Joe McCain told CNN that his brother plans to join his father and great-grandfather as naval aviators. "His grandfather, JSM Jr., was in submarines, commanding three different boats in World War II," he said. That grandfather later became Adm. In an interview last year with GoMids.com, Jack McCain reflected on the advice his father gave him on the day he arrived at the Naval Academy. "My dad told me there is one thing McCains are good at, and that is not giving in to pressure, and honor -- keeping our honor regardless of what happens," Jack McCain said. "He then said, 'Don't lie, cheat or steal -- anything else is fair game.' " John McCain, the Republican presidential nominee in 2008, frequently poked fun at his record at the Naval Academy while on the campaign trail, pointing out that he "stood fifth from the bottom" of his class and racked up dozens of demerits. McCain told Fox News on Thursday that his son is graduating "in better class standing than I had, which wasn't hard to do." "I'm very proud of him," he said. Meghan McCain, Jack's older sister, sent a message on Twitter Friday saying her younger brother, Jimmy, could not attend because he is serving overseas. McCain told Fox News he is returning home this weekend. In his remarks to the students, Obama made a vow that he would not send them to war unless it is "absolutely necessary." "It's a promise that as long as I am your commander in chief, I will only send you into harm's way when it is absolutely necessary, and with the strategy, the well-defined goals, the equipment and the support that you need to get the job done," he said. "This includes the job of bringing the Iraq war to a responsible end and pursuing a new comprehensive strategy to disrupt, dismantle and defeat al Qaeda and its allies in Afghanistan and Pakistan." Obama also promised additional assistance to military families, vowing that "we will be with you every step of the way, increasing your pay, increasing child care and helping families deal with the stress and separation of war." And he said new laws will help ensure that veterans are well taken care of. Obama's commencement address was his third and final of the year. He was also commencement speaker at Arizona State University and the University of Notre Dame.

John Sidney McCain IV, better known as Jack, became the fourth McCain—and the fourth to bear the same name—to graduate from the service academy in Annapolis, Maryland.

“America, look at these young men and women. Look at these sailors and Marines. Here are the values that we cherish. Here are the ideals that endure,” Obama told the crowd.

At about midday, during the academy’s commissioning and graduation ceremony, McCain received a Bachelor of Science degree, took the oath of office and was commissioned as an ensign in the U.S. Navy—103 years after his great-grandfather did the same.

Watch Obama hug John McCain’s son »

With his parents, John and Cindy McCain, looking on, Jack shook hands with President Obama before returning to the crowd amid applause and more hugs.

Joe McCain told CNN that Jack plans to follow his father and great-grandfather into naval aviation.

“His grandfather, JSM Jr., was in submarines, commanding three different boats in World War II,” he said.

That grandfather later became Adm. McCain and served as commander of the Pacific Theater during the Vietnam War, when Jack’s father, now Arizona Sen. John McCain, was being held as a prisoner of war in Hanoi.

In an interview last year with GoMids.com, Jack McCain reflected on the advice his father gave him on the day he arrived at the Naval Academy.

“My dad told me there is one thing McCains are good at, and that is not giving in to pressure, and honor—keeping our honor regardless of what happens,” Jack McCain said. “He then said, ‘Don’t lie, cheat or steal—anything else is fair game.’”

John McCain, the Republican presidential nominee in 2008, frequently joked about his own record at the Naval Academy while on the campaign trail, noting that he “stood fifth from the bottom” of his class and accumulated dozens of demerits.

At a campaign event last October, McCain joked that Jack needed a “DNA check” because he had yet to receive a single demerit. Jack later told GoMids.com that he had, in fact, accumulated some demerits—for wearing flip-flops outside and forgetting to shave.

McCain told Fox News on Thursday that his son was graduating “in better class standing than I had, which wasn’t hard to do.”

“I’m very proud of him,” he said.

Meghan McCain, Jack’s older sister, posted a message on Twitter Friday saying that their younger brother, Jimmy, could not attend because he was serving overseas. McCain told Fox News that Jimmy was returning home that weekend.

In his remarks to the graduates, Obama vowed that he would not send them to war unless it was “absolutely necessary.”

“It’s a promise that as long as I am your commander in chief, I will only send you into harm’s way when it is absolutely necessary, and with the strategy, the well-defined goals, the equipment and the support that you need to get the job done,” he said.

“This includes the job of bringing the Iraq war to a responsible end and pursuing a new comprehensive strategy to disrupt, dismantle and defeat al Qaeda and its allies in Afghanistan and Pakistan.”

Obama also promised additional assistance for military families, pledging that “we will be with you every step of the way, increasing your pay, increasing child care and helping families deal with the stress and separation of war.”

He added that new laws would help ensure that veterans receive proper care.

The Naval Academy speech was Obama’s third and final commencement address of the year. He also delivered commencement speeches at Arizona State University and the University of Notre Dame.

## Obama Addresses Naval Academy Graduates as Another McCain Joins the Fleet

When President Barack Obama spoke to the U.S. Naval Academy’s graduating class in Annapolis on May 22, 2009, he addressed young officers preparing to enter a military already engaged in wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Among the newly commissioned ensigns was John Sidney “Jack” McCain IV, continuing one of the best-known traditions of military service in American history.

### Obama’s message to the Class of 2009

In his first Naval Academy commencement address as commander in chief, Obama emphasized the seriousness of the graduates’ new responsibilities. They would be entering a security environment shaped not only by conventional warfare, he said, but also by terrorism, nuclear proliferation, piracy, cyber threats and instability in weak states.

Obama promised that he would not send American service members into danger casually. He said force should be used only when necessary, under a sound strategy and with clearly defined objectives. When military action was required, he pledged to provide troops with the equipment, leadership and support needed to complete their missions.

The president also connected national security with American principles. The United States did not have to choose between protecting itself and upholding the rule of law, he argued. In a period marked by debate over detention, interrogation and the treatment of terrorism suspects, Obama told the graduates that American values were a source of strength rather than an obstacle to security.

He also reminded them that military leadership required personal integrity. Their commissions would give them authority over sailors and Marines, but that authority came with an obligation to earn trust, accept responsibility and care for those under their command.

Obama acknowledged the sacrifices already being made by military families and noted that some members of the graduating class had relatives serving in combat. His broader message was that the country owed its service members more than praise: it owed them clear missions, adequate resources and lasting support after they returned home.

### Jack McCain becomes a Navy ensign

One of the graduates receiving a commission that day was Jack McCain, the son of Senator John McCain of Arizona, Obama’s Republican opponent in the 2008 presidential election.

Jack McCain graduated from the Naval Academy and was commissioned as an ensign, the Navy’s entry-level commissioned-officer rank. His father and mother, Cindy McCain, attended the ceremony. Obama’s presence gave the occasion an added political dimension—the sitting president was helping commission the son of the man he had defeated only months earlier—but the event also reflected a tradition both men frequently emphasized: military service transcending party politics.

Jack McCain later trained as a naval aviator and served as a helicopter pilot. His commissioning was notable not simply because he was the son of a prominent senator and presidential nominee, but because it extended a family connection to the Navy that reached back more than a century.

### A family shaped by naval service

The McCain family’s military history spans multiple generations.

Jack’s father, John Sidney McCain III, graduated from the Naval Academy in 1958 and became a naval aviator. During the Vietnam War, his aircraft was shot down over Hanoi in October 1967. Badly injured, he was captured and held as a prisoner of war for more than five years.

When North Vietnamese officials learned that his father was a senior Navy commander, they offered McCain early release. He refused to leave ahead of prisoners who had been captured before him, in keeping with the military’s code of conduct. He endured torture and prolonged imprisonment before being released in 1973. After retiring from the Navy as a captain, he entered politics, serving in the House of Representatives and then the Senate.

John McCain III’s father, Admiral John Sidney McCain Jr., was a submariner who rose to four-star rank. He served in senior commands during several Cold War conflicts and was commander in chief of U.S. Pacific Command while his son was imprisoned in North Vietnam.

Jack McCain’s great-grandfather, Admiral John Sidney McCain Sr., was also a four-star admiral and an early advocate of naval aviation. During World War II, he commanded aircraft-carrier forces in the Pacific. He died shortly after attending the Japanese surrender ceremony in September 1945.

The elder two McCains became the first father and son in the Navy’s history to attain four-star admiral rank. Their names were later joined on the guided-missile destroyer USS *John S. McCain*, which honors John McCain Sr., John McCain Jr. and, following a 2018 rededication, Senator John McCain III.

The tradition also extended beyond Jack. His brother James McCain served as a Marine and deployed to Iraq, while other members of the extended family have served in uniform as well.

### Service across generations

Jack McCain’s commissioning placed him within a lineage that included carrier aviation, submarine service, wartime command, combat flying and captivity. Yet Obama’s address made clear that family history alone did not define any new officer. Each graduate would have to establish his or her own record through judgment, character and service.

For the McCain family, the Annapolis ceremony represented continuity. For Obama, it was an opportunity to describe the obligations shared by civilian leaders and military officers: leaders must use force responsibly, while those entrusted with command must uphold both the nation’s security and its ideals.
